title: The Kettle & Crumb
part: PART ONE: SIXTY-ONE CHIMNEYS AND ONE TROLL

pages.text:
*From the Bridgewater Almanac: A well-run household has three rules: be quiet, be quick and be back before dark.*

The Kettle & Crumb smelled of burnt sugar and clove oil. It was a thick, warm smell, the kind that stuck to the back of your throat. Gran Wilhelmina stood behind the counter, her silver bun bristling with pencils and a small paintbrush. Her half-moon glasses slid down her nose. She wiped the brass register with a rag.

Flour dusted her sleeves to the elbows. She looked like a loaf that had lost a fight with a bag of flour.

"Sit down, you’ll fall down," she told the Mayor.

He hovered by the door, top hat in one hand, worry on his round face.

"The bridge, Wilhelmina," the Mayor said, tapping his foot. "The stones are loose. I feel a draft right through my wool."

Gran did not look up from her polishing.

"Then buy a thicker wool, Ambrose. Or a coat. I have a good one in the back, three shillings off."

She said this to everyone. The baker, the postman, the children who lingered for a second cup of cocoa. It was her way of anchoring them to the earth. Or at least to the floorboards. They were old and creaky, and they did not much appreciate being jumped on.
pages.image: A round, quick woman with a silver bun stuck with pencils and half-moon glasses wiping a brass register, flour on her sleeves, speaking to a worried man in a top hat inside a cozy tea shop filled with steam and light.

pages.text:
Upstairs, the flat was quieter, smelling of lavender and dried herbs. Gran set a plate of cold scones on the table, the crumbs bouncing off the wood. "So," she said, leaning on the back of a chair. "How was the yard today, Rue? Did the sun shine?"

"Fine," Rue said. She had practiced this word in the mirror that morning. It was smooth and round, like a stone that had been rolled by the river for a very long time. "Just fine. The chestnut tree dropped a lot of leaves. Cedric told a story about a sheep."

Gran’s eyes, which were sharp behind the glasses, narrowed just a fraction. She did not press. She knew Rue’s face when it was working hard, pulling the corners of the mouth up to keep the rest of the expression in check. She simply poured the tea, the steam rising in a lazy spiral, and let the silence do its work.

"Right then," Rue said, because her throat felt tight and she needed a sound that was not a question.

Gran nodded. She did not believe her. But she let her keep it, which was a kindness Rue was not sure she deserved, and which made the lie feel heavier than the truth ever had.
pages.image: A small, sturdy girl with curly red-brown hair in two puffs tied with green yarn sitting at a wooden table, looking down at a plate of scones, while an older woman with a silver bun watches her with a calm, knowing expression.

pages.text:
The river post did not come by foot, but by barge, and it arrived with a splash of water against the shop window. A damp envelope, brown and stiff with dried river mud, sat on the counter. Rue knew the handwriting before she opened it. It was tall and looping, the kind of writing that seemed to be moving even when the paper was still.

*Dear Rue,* it said. *The Persistent is stuck behind a very rude sandbank. The river is being stubborn, like a mule that has forgotten it is a mule. I will be home by the Founders' Fair, if the river behaves. Send a scone.*

Rue read it once. Then again. Then a third time, until the ink seemed to blur into a warm brown haze. She folded the letter carefully, smoothing the creases with her thumbs. She tucked it into her pocket, right next to her heart, where it pressed against her ribs with a solid, hopeful weight.

If Mari was coming home, then the town was not just a place where people walked the long way round. It was a place where a girl waited for her mother to dock at the end of the river.
pages.image: A girl in a patched mustard-yellow raincoat holding a brown envelope with both hands, reading it with a serious, hopeful expression, standing in front of a window with raindrops on the glass, her red-brown hair puffs visible.

pages.text:
Later, while Gran dozed in the armchair with a book tucked under her chin, Rue went to the dresser to find a clean handkerchief. The wood was dark and polished. There was one drawer that never opened. It had a small brass latch, tarnished green with age, and a lock that looked as though it had been turned many times by careful hands.

She did not touch it. She had made a rule about that, too.

But that night, as Gran moved the book to the nightstand and yawned, stretching her arms above her head, Rue saw her hand go to the latch. The sound of the lock clicking open was small. It filled the room like a bell. Gran pulled out a single object. It was a horn button, large as a saucer, the color of dark amber. She held it up to the light, turning it slowly. Her fingers traced the edge. Her face was very still. Very far away.

Then she put it back. Locked the drawer. Blew out the lamp.
pages.image: An older woman with a silver bun holding a large, round, amber-colored button up to the light, her expression solemn and distant, standing in a dimly lit bedroom with a closed wooden dresser in the background.

pages.text:
Biscuit was already on Rue’s feet, a warm, purring loaf of orange fur. The cat stretched, yawned a yawn that lasted for three seconds, and settled into a tight coil. Rue lay on her back, staring at the ceiling, listening to the town settle. A window creaked open on the other side of the street. A dog barked twice, then stopped. The river murmured, a low, constant sound that seemed to come from everywhere and nowhere.

She thought about the old bridge. She thought about the moss, and the way the stones were uneven, and the fact that nobody walked on it. Had anyone ever looked under it? Really looked? Not to count the sheep, or to check for wool, but just to see what was there.

Right then, she told herself. You haven’t thought that. You are tired. You are going to sleep.

But the image of the dark space under the arch stayed with her, waiting in the corner of her mind, patient as a cat.
pages.image: A small girl with curly red-brown hair in two puffs lying in bed, eyes wide, looking at the ceiling, while a large orange cat is curled up on her feet, the room dimly lit by a window showing a night sky.
